risk_of_bias.note: Seen only through three narrative reviews (cards sc_moeller_2017: high; sc_verstraete_2004: high; sc_saitman_2014: some concerns, but it leaves false negatives out and only names them). The 2017 review's statements on what screens miss cite studies whose designs, samples and results it does not describe (laboratory studies of what screens react to, comparisons of methods, validation studies, a textbook chapter and older reviews); its Table 4 comes from the authors' 2008 review without tests, concentrations or frequencies, and its selection is unsystematic. The 2014 review's two sentences on false negatives cite another review and one paper. The 2004 review's flunitrazepam result is one study whose size and immunoassays are not given.

inconsistency.note: The three reviews agree in direction (opiate and benzodiazepine screens can miss drugs of their own class) and cite different sources on the point; none reports a screen that reliably found fentanyl, methadone, buprenorphine, lorazepam, alprazolam or clonazepam. One tension inside the 2017 review (its text names hydrocodone and hydromorphone among opioids that may be missed, its table lists them among possible positives) is reported in the statement.

indirectness.note: Second-hand and dated: the statements concern unnamed 'most' or 'commonly marketed' screens, US workplace rules and laboratory practice up to 2016, with the table adapted from 2008; screens sold since, or in other countries, may differ (the 2017 review itself notes newer amphetamine screens that no longer react to a nasal inhaler). The flunitrazepam result is one study of a single dose given by researchers.

imprecision.note: Not rated separately: the claim gives no frequency, because the reviews print none for how often a screen misses a drug a person took (the one figure, a 12% rise in false negatives when one synthetic cannabinoid test's cutoff was raised, has no stated base); the statement says that how often is unknown.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

rate.reasoning: Descriptive (which drugs standard urine screens are built for and which they can miss), seen only through narrative reviews: start low (METHODS §6.3: a claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies they describe, here mostly laboratory studies of what screens react to, and is rated down for risk of bias and indirectness); risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 take it to very low, the floor. It rests only on narrative reviews, so it stays at draft and says that its figures are second-hand. The rule for test accuracy (METHODS §6.3) was considered and not applied: the claim says which drugs screens are reported to miss, not how often a test reads right, and no review gives accuracy figures for any screen and drug. The comparisons the reviews cite (for example clonazepam by immunoassay against LC-MS/MS, five immunoassays for alprazolam and triazolam, an ELISA for synthetic cannabinoids) would start high under that rule, but seen only as the reviews' sentences, without samples or results, they would be rated down two levels for risk of bias and one for indirectness, to very low as well. Status replicated: separate primary sources described in the reviews agree that benzodiazepine screens miss some benzodiazepines (more positives for alprazolam and triazolam with a lower cutoff and an enzyme step, Fraser and Meatherall, in the 2017 review; immunoassays never positive after a single dose of flunitrazepam, Kintz et al., in the 2004 review; and the 2014 review's citation of Mikel et al.), and the 2017 and 2014 reviews agree that opiate screens miss some opioids; the sentences on fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine rest on the 2017 review alone, which cites two studies it does not describe. The reviews cite different sources on misses (the 2017 review cites the 2004 review only for detection times). Nothing is phrased as advice on avoiding or passing a test, on timing or on amounts: the reviews' sections on tampering with samples and on detection times were not used, and the 2017 review's reason for the benzodiazepine cutoffs, given in prescribed amounts, and the dose in the flunitrazepam study are left out.

(2017): most panels cover the five US federal workplace drugs (amphetamines, cocaine, marijuana, opiates, phencyclidine), with benzodiazepines commonly included; Table 4 (adapted from the authors' 2008 review; no tests, concentrations or frequencies), may not be detected: opioid screens, buprenorphine, fentanyl, meperidine, methadone, oxycodone, oxymorphone and tramadol; benzodiazepine screens, alprazolam, clonazepam and lorazepam; cannabinoid screens, nabilone and synthetic cannabinoids; 'not applicable' for the alcohol, amphetamine, cocaine, phencyclidine, tricyclic antidepressant and synthetic cannabinoid screens. Opiate screens: morphine the single calibrator; low cross-reactivity with oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone and oxymorphone; no reactivity of fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine in commonly marketed morphine-specific immunoassays; federal workplace opiate cutoff 2000 ng/mL (300 ng/mL before 1998), with 300 ng/mL suggested for monitoring prescribed opioids. Benzodiazepine screens: built for free oxazepam or nordiazepam; glucuronide conjugates (lorazepam, alprazolam) not detected by most immunoassays without beta-glucuronidase hydrolysis, which most laboratories do not use; cutoffs 200 or 300 ng/mL; lowering the alprazolam and triazolam cutoff to 100 ng/mL with hydrolysis increased positives (Fraser and Meatherall; no counts given); 40 ng/mL recommended for 7-aminoclonazepam (West et al.); the authors describe a high rate of false negatives, with no figure. Synthetic cannabinoids: no accepted cutoff (assays 5 to 25 ng/mL); one ELISA for JWH-018 metabolites (Barnes et al.), 73 synthetic cannabinoids tested, false negatives up 12% (base not stated) when the cutoff was raised from 5 to 10 µg/L; newer compounds PB-22, RCS-4, RCS-8, XRL-11 and AKB48 detected with limitations. Synthetic cathinones: one immunoassay (Randox Drugs of Abuse V biochip), mephedrone and MDPV concentrations below acceptance criteria with high negative bias. Saitman et al. (2014): opiate and benzodiazepine immunoassays have clinically important false negatives, no figures; false negatives outside the review.

lines.statement: Standard urine drug screens can miss some drugs, including fentanyl and other synthetic or semisynthetic opioids on opiate screens, and some benzodiazepines, alprazolam (Xanax) among them, on benzodiazepine screens, as described second-hand in three narrative reviews: a clinical review for clinicians (Moeller et al., 2017; literature from 1946 to 2016; its table of drugs that screens may not detect is adapted from a 2008 review by three of its four authors), a laboratory review of false positives that names false negatives as a problem but leaves them out (Saitman et al., 2014), and a single-author review of detection times (Verstraete, 2004). Screens are immunoassays, run in a laboratory or on the spot, whose antibodies in general react to drugs' breakdown products or classes of them; on-the-spot tests have the same limits as laboratory ones. By the 2017 review, which drugs a panel covers depends on the setting: most include the five drugs of the US federal workplace rules (amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, opiates and PCP), benzodiazepines are commonly added, and clinicians treating pain are advised to consider added tests for semisynthetic opioids such as oxycodone and synthetic ones such as fentanyl and methadone. Opioids: most opiate screens use morphine to set the line between positive and negative, and their antibodies react little with oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone and oxymorphone, so these may be missed; fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine differ from morphine in structure, commonly marketed morphine-specific screens do not react to them, and finding them needs a screen made for each or LC-MS/MS; some laboratories do not test for semisynthetic or synthetic opioids in a standard opioid screen unless specially asked. The review's table lists buprenorphine, fentanyl, meperidine, methadone, oxycodone, oxymorphone and tramadol as possibly not detected on opioid screens (its text adds that GC-MS, LC-MS/MS and other methods to measure tramadol in urine have been developed); the review gives the commonest reasons for a false-negative opioid result as a test that is wrong for the opioid or too little of it in the urine, and says that the high US workplace cutoff for opiates can give negative results that make recent opioid use hard to interpret, especially for synthetic and semisynthetic opioids. Benzodiazepines: most benzodiazepine screens are built to detect the free forms of oxazepam or nordiazepam, breakdown products shared by diazepam and several others; many benzodiazepines, among them lorazepam and alprazolam, are excreted bound to glucuronic acid and are not detected by most screens unless the urine is first treated with an enzyme (beta-glucuronidase), which most laboratories do not do; clonazepam, broken down mainly to 7-aminoclonazepam, reacts poorly; the usual cutoffs, first set for older benzodiazepines, are often too high for lorazepam, alprazolam and triazolam, and one team found more positives for alprazolam and triazolam with a lower cutoff and the enzyme step; a screen cannot tell one benzodiazepine from another; and the review speaks of a high rate of false negatives without giving a figure. The 2014 review says that opiate and benzodiazepine screens have clinically important false negatives, citing other papers without discussing them, and that the many testing platforms differ in what they react to. Newer drugs: cannabis screens do not detect synthetic cannabinoids (nor the prescribed cannabinoid nabilone); tests made for synthetic cannabinoids mostly target breakdown products of JWH-018 and JWH-073, with broader detection where other compounds share the same 'structural pathway' (the review's words), but new compounds keep appearing, and in one study such a test was limited in detecting several newer ones; attempts to detect synthetic cathinones ('bath salts') in urine had not given good results, one immunoassay with antibodies for mephedrone and MDPV measuring them below acceptance criteria in validation studies, and the review expects that detecting particular cathinones will need more specific methods such as high-resolution mass spectrometry (it also calls the parent drugs easily detected in biological materials, without naming the method); and salvia can be tested in urine only by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS and, being costly and complex to test, is not routinely tested. A negative screen does not show that a drug is absent: a result below the cutoff is reported as negative and means only that the level was below the cutoff (2017 review), and a negative opiate screen says nothing about fentanyl, to which morphine-specific screens do not react. Where the reviews say what finds a drug that a screen misses, it is a test made for that drug, a changed screening procedure (for benzodiazepines, the enzyme step with a lower cutoff) or chromatography with mass spectrometry (GC-MS, LC-MS/MS), the most sensitive methods raising the chance of detection (2004 review); but the 2017 review says GC-MS is costly and therefore kept for confirming positive screens, and the 2014 review that mass spectrometry is limited or absent in many hospital laboratories and its results usually take several days. The reviews give no figure for how often a screen misses a drug that a person took (the one number is a 12% rise in false negatives, its base not stated, when one synthetic cannabinoid test's cutoff was raised), name few tests, and date from 2004, 2014 and 2017; tests change (the 2017 review notes newer amphetamine screens no longer giving a false positive with a nasal inhaler), so these papers cannot say which drugs today's screens cover. The three reviews agree in direction, and none contradicts another on what screens miss; within the 2017 review, the text names hydrocodone and hydromorphone among opioids that opiate screens may miss, while its table lists them among possible positives and not among drugs that may not be detected. How well urine test strips find fentanyl or benzodiazepines when used to check drugs themselves is covered in the answers on drug checking. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

lines.q: Can a drug test miss fentanyl, or benzos like Xanax?
lines.short: Yes. Expert reviews say standard opiate tests don't react to fentanyl at all. Most benzo tests can miss Xanax (alprazolam) unless the lab adds an extra step.
lines.but: This is about urine tests, from expert reviews dated 2004 to 2017, not new studies. They give no numbers on how often a drug is missed, and tests change.
how: Quick urine tests, in a lab or on the spot, look only for what they're built to find. Most cover amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, opiates and PCP, often benzos too. Cannabis tests don't catch synthetic cannabinoids, and tests for 'bath salts' haven't worked well.

Most opiate tests are set up for morphine. Fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine don't react with them, and oxycodone only weakly. These need tests of their own, and some labs don't run them unless asked.
Most benzo tests can miss lorazepam and alprazolam (Xanax) unless the lab first treats the urine with an enzyme. Most labs don't. Clonazepam reacts poorly.

A negative only means the level was under the test's cutoff, or the test doesn't react to that drug. Lab tests like mass spectrometry find more. But they cost more and are mostly used to check positives. Many hospital labs can do little or none of it.
